motivation:
The combinational ALU currently describes three independent 64-bit products for
signed-signed, unsigned-unsigned, and signed-unsigned multiplication. All three
exist in the synthesized datapath even though a single-issue instruction can use
only one multiply result, consuming scarce LUTs and routing resources on a design
already at 9563 LUT4s and likely depressing Fmax.

title: Move DIV and REM into a cold iterative execution unit
motivation:
The current single-cycle ALU places four 32-bit division and remainder
expressions in the execute datapath. On an FPGA these operators expand into
large combinational networks that consume scarce LUTs and routing and burden
Fmax on every cycle, even though divide-class instructions are rare in the
timed CoreMark workload. The core is already close to its LUT4 target, so
removing this cold logic from the one-cycle path should improve both timing
and placement freedom at little workload-cycle cost.

combinational divider from the critical path raises median FPGA Fmax.

title: Tiny tagged BTB with direction counters
motivation:
Every taken branch or jump is currently discovered in EX, after two younger
instructions have entered the front end and must be discarded. CoreMark has
frequent loop backedges and control-flow transfers, so this fixed redirect
penalty directly reduces iterations per cycle. A small BTB supplies an
already-computed target and therefore keeps target generation out of the
fetch critical path, which is important because fitness also scales with
FPGA Fmax and the design is close to its LUT target.

title: Qualify load-use hazards by actual source operands
motivation:
The load-use detector compares a load destination against both raw rs1 and
rs2 bitfields of the following instruction. Those fields are not both source
registers for many RV32 formats: OP-IMM, loads, and JALR do not read rs2,
while LUI, AUIPC, and JAL read neither field. Coincidental matches therefore
inject unnecessary bubbles into CoreMark without protecting any dependency.

sequential fetch stream reveals PC+4 one cycle before that instruction is

motivation:
The combined backward-branch and JAL static predictor cut CoreMark cycles by
about five percent and finished only 0.20 percent below its then-best fitness,

direction logic, two immediate formats, and a full predicted-PC value carried
through the front end. Direct JAL is a narrower opportunity: it is always
taken and its target is encoded in the fetched instruction, so it needs no
learned state and cannot suffer a direction misprediction.

motivation:

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one learned backward-branch entry containing the exact branch PC, resolved
target PC, target-plus-four PC, and the first instruction at the target. When
an accepted fetch matches the entry, latch a fold-pending bit rather than
changing the PC immediately. On the following cycle, inject the registered
target instruction and its target PC into decode while the fetch PC advances
from registered target-plus-four. Thus the exact-PC comparison ends at a
register, and the next-PC path sees only registered state: no tag lookup,
instruction decode, target adder, counter, or predicted-target selection is
placed in the lookup cycle's PC recurrence. Carry a folded-prediction bit with
the branch so EX suppresses its redirect only when the branch is actually
taken to the stored target; a loop exit or stale entry flushes the injected
instruction and redirects to the architectural fall-through. Fill the cached
target instruction from the first ready imem response after a qualifying EX
redirect, and invalidate or defer folding across stalls so no response is
duplicated or lost. This should remove the two-bubble penalty from repetitions
of the hottest inner loop while attacking the timing mechanism that defeated
all direct next-PC predictors.
